prompt.context: Your client is a large retail-focused private equity firm that owns Salty Sole, a leading designer of junior women's footwear, primarily targeting the 14–22 year old age group. Salty Sole was purchased last year by the private equity firm expecting to realize substantial profits upon sale in 2012 by increasing the company's EBITDA. The situation, however, is that due to a current recession, annual profit has only grown modestly post the acquisition and is not on track to generate the double-digit returns that the private equity firm originally anticipated.
prompt.question: How can the company increase profitability and achieve the private equity firm's return on investment objectives?

clarifying_info.q: Who are Salty Sole's customers / what channel does it sell through?
clarifying_info.a: Client designs and distributes footwear to discount retailers (think Kohl's) and is considered mid-priced.

clarifying_info.q: Does Salty Sole manufacture its own shoes?
clarifying_info.a: Client outsources all manufacturing on a fixed-contract basis; manufacturing costs with outsourced providers fall under Fixed Costs.

clarifying_info.q: How does Salty Sole compete — does it lead fashion trends?
clarifying_info.a: Client follows a 'me-too' strategy, follows fashion rather than inventing it, then offers lower prices than name brands. It competes on trendy fashion and value pricing.

clarifying_info.q: What markets does Salty Sole operate in?
clarifying_info.a: Client is the market leader in junior women's footwear in the U.S. only.

clarifying_info.q: What is the average selling price per unit?
clarifying_info.a: Pricing has remained constant at an average of $25 per unit. The company has determined it would not be prudent to adjust pricing based on industry research.

clarifying_info.q: What is the target sale value / return for the private equity firm?
clarifying_info.a: A 20% return on investment requires approximately a $300 million sale value in 2012.

exhibits.title: Salty Sole Financial Estimates 2006–2012
exhibits.shows: A table of annual financials from 2006A through 2012E showing Sales, Discounts/Allowances, Net Sales, % change in Net Sales, Cost of Goods Sold, Fixed Costs, Total Costs, EBITDA, a 6.5x Sale Multiple, and resulting Purchase/Sale Price and Return on Investment.

exhibits.title: U.S. Casual Footwear Market Size and Share 2006–2009
exhibits.shows: A stacked bar chart showing percent market share for Salty Sole and five named competitors in the U.S. casual footwear market from 2006 to 2009, with total market size labeled above each bar.

framework: Revenue = Price x Volume (net of Discounts/Allowances)
Price: assess current pricing, elasticity, brand equity implications of any change
Volume: assess current unit sales, addressable market, and growth levers
Costs: Fixed costs (manufacturing contracts, overhead) vs. Variable costs (COGS as % of sales)
Since both price and costs are currently constrained, isolate volume as the key driver
Quantify the volume required to hit the PE firm's target EBITDA and test feasibility against market size/share data

questions.prompt: Looking at Exhibit 1, what observations can you make about Salty Sole's financial performance and cost structure?
questions.guidance: Strong answer: (1) Company grew rapidly pre-recession (2006–2007 net sales +30%) then declined and has only gradual recovery. (2) Discounts/Allowances stay at 1% of sales throughout — no incremental discounting pressure. (3) Variable costs (COGS) remain flat at ~50% of net sales throughout all years. (4) Fixed costs are flat at $15M per year (~23–25% of net sales). (5) EBITDA has not recovered to pre-recession levels and the 2012E projection falls far short of what the PE firm needs.

questions.prompt: The PE firm needs a 20% return, implying a $300M sale value in 2012. How many pairs of shoes must Salty Sole sell in 2012 to make that happen? (Assume average price = $25/unit, ignore discounts/allowances for simplicity, variable cost = 50% of revenue, fixed costs = $15M, sale multiple = 6.5x EBITDA.)
questions.guidance: Candidate should work backwards from target sale value to required EBITDA, then set up the profit equation solving for volume. Should note that the required volume is more than double the 2008–2009 levels and flag that feasibility depends on market size/share.

math.setup: Target sale value = $300M; Sale multiple = 6.5x; so required EBITDA = $300M / 6.5 ≈ $46.15M, round to $50M. EBITDA = Revenue – Variable Costs – Fixed Costs = 25v – 0.5*25*v – 15,000,000
math.answer: 5,200,000 pairs of shoes must be sold in 2012

questions.prompt: Is achieving 5.2 million units feasible given the market? (Hand out Exhibit 2.)
questions.guidance: Candidate should note: (1) Salty Sole is already the market leader with >35% share of the U.S. casual footwear market. (2) The total market is roughly flat at ~$57–58B with no projected growth. (3) Organic volume growth through market share gains alone will be very difficult. (4) This implies the company must pursue new products, new categories, new geographies, or new distribution channels to hit the volume target.

questions.prompt: Given that cost structure is fixed and pricing is fixed, what strategies could Salty Sole pursue to achieve the required volume growth?
questions.guidance: Candidate should brainstorm credible growth levers and pair each with risks. Strong answers cover: new geographies (international expansion), new distribution channels (e-commerce, department stores), new product categories (adjacent footwear segments, accessories), increased marketing to steal share, acquisitions of complementary brands, and product mix shifts toward higher-margin items. Risks include capacity constraints, brand dilution, cannibalization, and execution risk in unfamiliar markets.

brainstorming.prompt: What strategies would you recommend Salty Sole pursue to more than double its unit volume and achieve the PE firm's return target?

categories.name: Volume — Steal Share
ideas: Increase marketing spend to gain share from competitors in existing U.S. market
Improve retailer placement and shelf space at discount retailers
Launch targeted digital/social campaigns for 14–22 age demographic

categories.name: Volume — New Distribution Channels
ideas: Launch or expand direct-to-consumer e-commerce channel
Enter department store or specialty retail channels

categories.name: Volume — New Geographies
ideas: International expansion (e.g., Canada, UK, emerging markets)
Geographic expansion within the U.S. to underpenetrated regions

categories.name: Volume — New Products / Categories
ideas: Expand into adjacent footwear categories (athletic, boots, sandals)
Add accessories or complementary products to grow basket size
Acquire a complementary brand with established distribution

categories.name: Price / Mix Improvement
ideas: Add premium features or limited-edition lines to support a slightly higher price tier
Shift product mix toward higher-margin SKUs
Bundle products to increase average transaction value

categories.name: Risks to Flag
ideas: Capacity constraints if outsourced manufacturing contracts cannot scale
Brand dilution risk if moving upmarket or expanding too broadly
Cannibalization if new product lines compete with existing portfolio
Execution risk and time-to-market in new geographies or channels
Recession environment limits consumer discretionary spending

recommendation: Since cost structure (fixed at $15M) and variable costs (50% of revenue) cannot be reduced further, and pricing is fixed at $25/unit, the only lever to achieve the PE firm's $300M exit value is increasing volume from the current trajectory to 5.2 million units — more than double recent levels.

Given that the U.S. casual footwear market is flat and Salty Sole already holds >35% share, organic domestic volume growth alone is insufficient; the company must pursue a combination of international expansion, new distribution channels (e-commerce, new retail formats), and potentially adjacent product categories or brand acquisitions to reach the required volume.
risks: Reaching 5.2M units requires entering new markets or channels where the company has no established presence, creating execution and investment risk
The recession environment suppresses consumer discretionary spending, making volume growth especially challenging
Expanding product lines or categories risks cannibalization and brand dilution
Manufacturing partners on fixed contracts may not have capacity to scale to 5.2M units without renegotiation
next_steps: Conduct detailed market sizing for international markets and new U.S. distribution channels to identify the highest-ROI volume growth paths
Assess manufacturing capacity and flexibility to scale to 5.2M units
Evaluate M&A targets that could provide incremental volume and distribution access quickly
Model the economics of a direct-to-consumer e-commerce launch given the 14–22 age demographic's online behavior
